implementation_notes: Rust has no named or default arguments, so configuration is a struct plus `Default`: implement `Default` with the intended values, then build the options with functional update syntax - `Options { port: 9000, ..Options::default() }` - or accept the options struct directly, which is plain standard-library style. Builders (bon, derive_builder, typed-builder) add per-member defaults (`#[builder(default = ...)]`), compile-time requiredness (typestate) and `maybe_`-style optional setters when the option set is large or construction is staged; a plain `#[derive(Default)]` only yields zero/empty values, so the hand-written `Default` impl is where real defaults belong.
pitfalls: `..base` moves the fields it does not copy: for non-`Copy` fields the base value is partially moved and cannot be used afterwards, so functional update is best for short-lived options values (clone explicitly if the base must survive).
A derived `Default` produces zero/empty values (0, "", None), which may be invalid or semantically wrong for the API; implement `Default` by hand or use per-field builder defaults.

Struct update syntax requires every field to be visible, so an options struct with private fields - or a #[non_exhaustive] one from another crate - cannot be updated functionally; expose `with_*` methods or a builder instead.

Builder typestate encodes requiredness in the type, but the generated builder is part of the public API: changing a member from required to optional, or the crate's MSRV, is a breaking change for callers.

variants.name: Derive builders with per-member defaults (bon, derive_builder, typed-builder)
variants.implementation_notes: When options are numerous, staged, or must report missing required settings at compile time, a derive macro generates a builder from the options struct/function: `#[builder(default)]` marks optional members, `Option<T>` members become optional automatically, required members are enforced by the typestate, and setters accept `impl Into<T>`. bon reports that adding `#[builder(default)]` or switching between `Option<T>` and a defaulted member is backward compatible, and builder crates can also generate the builder for a function (`#[builder] fn new(...)`) so callers get named, defaulted construction without a hand-written struct.
pitfalls: Each derive macro adds a compile-time dependency and a generated API whose error messages and MSRV are controlled by the crate.
Generated builders are part of the public API surface: adding a `#[builder(default)]` member is easy, but reordering/renaming members or changing requiredness breaks callers.
Setters taking `impl Into<T>` accept one value per call flag; when used in generic code they can defeat type inference and force turbofish.
